title: Chunked Budget Allocation Prevents Non-Monotonic Regressions in World-Model Verification

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution identifies why increasing verification budget can paradoxically reduce agent task success in sequential verify-and-retry workflows. No prior paper explicitly establishes this relationship. While [19] discusses false negatives in verification and their impact on reinforcement learning, it does not address the paradoxical reduction in task success due to increased verification budgets. Similarly, [22] explores retry patterns and their impact on application performance but does not connect retries to verification budget increases or task success reduction. Therefore, no prior paper reports or establishes the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism
The contribution names and characterizes trajectory drift, where the agent re-browses after a verification rejection and frequently selects a worse product than originally found. [3] discusses retries in voice search queries, identifying user behavior when adapting to system failures, but does not characterize trajectory drift or its specific impact on task success. [19] highlights false negatives in verification but does not describe the mechanism of trajectory drift or its consequences. [10] addresses verification-aware planning but focuses on multi-agent collaboration challenges rather than trajectory drift. None of the prior papers substantively match the described mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates trajectory drift, showing it accounts for 60.5% of failures when agents re-browse after verification rejection. [8] discusses evaluating web agent trajectories but focuses on rule-based and human evaluation methods rather than quantifying trajectory drift. [15] introduces a benchmark for evaluating safety and trustworthiness in web agents but does not measure trajectory drift or its contribution to failures. [19] evaluates false negatives in verification but does not quantify their impact on trajectory drift. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design to measure this specific phenomenon.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of web agents and world-model verification. [7], [8], [15], and [19] all address web agents and verification-related challenges, establishing this as a known application area. While the specific sub-problem of trajectory drift is new, the general domain of web agents and verification is covered.

### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to prevent non-monotonic regressions by restructuring how a fixed verification budget is spent. None of the prior papers explicitly address this objective. While some papers discuss budget allocation (e.g., [7], [8], [12], [28]), their purposes differ. For example, [7] focuses on optimal rollout allocation for test-time policy optimization, and [8] introduces variance-informed predictive allocation for reinforcement learning. Neither explicitly targets preventing non-monotonic regressions. Similarly, [12] optimizes sample compute allocation for LLM inference, but its purpose is efficiency, not regression prevention. Thus, no prior paper shares the same purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves chunked budget allocation, where a fixed budget \( B \) is divided into \( M \) cycles, with \( K = B/M \) parallel rollouts per cycle. This mechanism is not explicitly covered by any prior paper. Papers like [7], [8], and [12] discuss adaptive or optimal allocation of budgets, but their mechanisms differ. For instance, [7] uses Bayesian sequential probability models, [8] employs variance-informed strategies, and [12] formulates allocation as a learning problem. None of these papers describe the specific mechanism of chunked budget allocation with parallel rollouts per cycle. Therefore, the mechanism is novel.

The evaluation uses WebShop to compare chunked verification (M = 1) against sequential verify-and-retry (M = 10), showing a 25x improvement at the same budget. This evaluation design is covered by [11], which compares parallel and sequential strategies for scaling test-time compute in LLM reasoning. Both evaluations involve comparing parallel and sequential strategies under matched budgets, even though the specific benchmarks differ (WebShop vs. reasoning benchmarks). Thus, the evaluation design is not novel.

### Domain
The domain is agent verification budget allocation, specifically in the WebShop environment. Papers like [7], [8], and [12] operate in similar domains involving budget allocation for agent or model verification tasks. For example, [7] and [8] address rollout allocation in reinforcement learning, and [12] focuses on sample compute allocation for LLM inference. While the specific instance (WebShop) is new, the general domain of agent verification budget allocation is covered. Therefore, the domain is not novel.
